spec.title: Accepted (202) rps by body size
spec.description: Events per second the server answered with 202, split by the SIZE tag of k6 (body bytes). In an 'over' run the plateau is the capacity of that size: look for where it drops. A flat line from 200 B to 10 KB and a drop only at 100 KB would mean fixed per-request cost dominates. Surprising: capacity falling already at 2 KB (the TOAST threshold). Added by B7: k6_b7_resp_202_total exists only after a k6 run.

spec.title: k6 offered rps (all requests sent)
spec.description: Requests per second k6 sent. In an 'at' run it should sit at the offered rate; if it is below the rate, k6 dropped iterations (see row 4). Compare with the accepted panel: the gap is the load the server did not take.

spec.title: Client latency p50 and p99 (k6)
spec.description: Latency seen by k6, by body size. Native histogram form (no _bucket series in Prometheus for k6). Expect p99 to blow up once the offered rate is above the capacity of that size (requests queue). Surprising: p50 rising with size in the 'at' runs by more than a few ms.

spec.title: Not accepted: 503 and other (413, 500, timeout)
spec.description: Responses that were not 202. 503 = the server shed the request (pool or DB trouble). 'other' includes a 413 if the body limit were too small and status 0 for timeouts. Expect 0 in the 'at' runs. Surprising: any 413 (BODY_LIMIT is set to 1mb for the measured runs). Added by B7 (k6 custom counters).

spec.title: Server request duration p99 (POST /v1/events)
spec.description: Latency measured inside the server, without k6 queueing. Compare with the k6 p99: the difference is time spent waiting before the server saw the request. Surprising: server p99 high while the pool wait is small (then the time is in Node CPU or in the query).

spec.title: WAL bytes per second
spec.description: How fast Postgres writes WAL (from the WAL position, exported by pg-wal-exporter.sh). WAL rate = accepted rps x WAL bytes per event. Expect it to grow with size even when rps falls. Surprising: WAL/s that stays flat from 10 KB to 100 KB (it would mean the disk is the limit).

spec.title: WAL bytes per inserted event
spec.description: WAL bytes divided by inserted events, the number I predicted per size. It should climb roughly with the body size above 2 KB. Includes full-page images and index records, so it is above the pure payload size. The exact per-size values from before/after snapshots are in summary.tsv (wal_B_per_row); this panel is the time view. Only meaningful while load runs.

spec.title: WAL full-page images and records per second
spec.description: Records written and full-page images (8 kB copies of a page after a checkpoint). A big body writes many TOAST chunk records per event. Surprising: FPI/s large compared with records/s.

spec.title: Table and index size of events (growth)
spec.description: Size of the events table (from postgres-exporter) and its indexes. Each run starts from an empty table (TRUNCATE), so the slope is the growth per event x rate. I did not check whether the exporter's table size includes the TOAST table; the exact heap/TOAST/index bytes per event are in summary.tsv (heap_B_per_row, toast_B_per_row, index_B_per_row). Index size per event should not change with payload size.

spec.title: Bytes into Postgres container disk (write) and host disk
spec.description: Disk write rate of the Postgres container (cgroup, from pg-container-exporter.sh) and of the host disks (node_exporter). WAL goes to disk at commit; heap and TOAST pages follow at checkpoint, so about 2x the WAL rate is possible. Surprising: container and host curves far apart (other disk users).

spec.title: Bytes on the wire: k6 sent (client side)
spec.description: Bytes per second k6 sends (headers + body). Network cost of the payload: about rps x body size. On localhost this is memory copies, not a real network, so it understates the cost of a real one.

spec.title: DB query time p99 and pool wait p99 (server)
spec.description: Time of the INSERT as seen by the server, and the wait for a pool connection. Big bodies should lengthen the INSERT (more bytes to send, parse, TOAST, WAL). If the pool wait grows too, the pool (25) is saturated because connections are held longer. Surprising: INSERT time flat but capacity down (then Node CPU is the limit).

spec.title: Pool connections: in use vs waiting
spec.description: Connections of the pg pool (max 25) in use, and callers waiting for one. In use = total - idle. Waiting above 0 for a long time means the pool is the bottleneck.

spec.title: Server CPU (pinned CPUs) user vs system
spec.description: Host CPU time on the server's pinned CPUs (0,6) by mode. JSON parsing and string copies are user time; moving bytes through sockets is system time. Node runs JS on one thread, so about 50% of the pair (one CPU) means Node is saturated. Surprising: system time growing faster than user time with size.

spec.expr: sum by (mode) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{job="node", cpu=~"$cpu_server", mode=~"user|system"}[$__rate_interval])) / count(count by (cpu) (node_cpu_seconds_total{job="node", cpu=~"$cpu_server"}))

spec.title: Postgres container CPU (cores)
spec.description: CPU seconds per second used by the Postgres container (4 CPUs available), by mode. Big values cost CPU in JSON text to jsonb conversion, compression attempts (pglz) and TOAST chunking. Surprising: more than 3 cores busy (Postgres would then be the limit).

spec.title: Event loop lag p99 and GC time
spec.description: Node event loop lag (p99) and the share of time spent in garbage collection. Big strings create garbage. Event loop lag above about 50 ms means Node itself is overloaded. Surprising: GC time growing a lot before the loop lag does.

spec.title: Host disk busy (io time)
spec.description: Share of time the host disks were busy. Close to 100% for the 100 KB runs would mean the disk limits throughput, not Node.

spec.title: Checkpoints and buffers written by checkpoint
spec.description: Requested checkpoints per second (max_wal_size is 1 GB, so heavy WAL forces them) and buffers written by checkpoints. Many requested checkpoints during the big-body runs mean full-page images repeat and the disk gets extra work. Surprising: no requested checkpoints with 100 KB events.

spec.title: Network bytes on the host (loopback + interfaces)
spec.description: Receive bytes per second on all host interfaces (loopback included). Traffic to the database container goes over docker's bridge, so this includes both the HTTP bytes and the INSERT bytes. Not a limit on one machine.

spec.title: k6 dropped iterations (must be 0 in 'at' runs)
spec.description: Iterations k6 could not start because all VUs were busy. In 'at' runs it should be 0; in 'over' runs it is expected (that is how I find the capacity). Surprising: drops in an 'at' run: the generator or the server is the limit.

spec.title: k6 failed requests share
spec.description: Share of requests that were not 202 (k6 counts only 202 as success). Should be 0 in 'at' runs.

spec.title: k6 CPU (pinned CPUs) busy
spec.description: Host CPU busy on the CPUs k6 is pinned to (3,4,9,10). Keep under about 70%, otherwise the generator slows down and hides the server's capacity. 100 KB bodies cost k6 more (building and sending the string), so watch it in those runs.

spec.title: k6 VUs in use vs max
spec.description: Virtual users in use. If it reaches the max (3000) in an 'at' run, the server answered too slowly for the open model to keep up.

spec.title: 1. The verdict: does throughput fall as the payload grows?
2. The mechanism: where do the bytes go?
3. Resource view: where does the cost land?
4. Validity checks: can I trust this run?
